passage:
Dear Rehana,
You remember I told you Mallika got the research grant I'd applied for? Since then I've been the nicest person in our lab. I brought her the good biscuits. I offered to proofread her budget. I told her twice how thrilled I was. Last Tuesday I caught myself wishing her printer would jam, and then instantly offering to fix it. That's when I stopped and actually sat with it, on the bus home.
The truth is, I'm jealous. I'm also truly glad it's her, because she worked on that proposal for a year. Both are true. Admitting that felt awful for about ten minutes, and then oddly light.
Yesterday I congratulated her again, just once, quietly, and asked what she'd do first with the money. We talked for an hour. It didn't feel like a performance.
Jyoti, the same girl who once sulked for a week when you got the lead in the college play

qa.q: What did Jyoti catch herself wishing last Tuesday?
qa.a: That Mallika's printer would jam.

qa.q: Why did being extra nice to Mallika feel right to Jyoti at first?
qa.a: The niceness covered a jealousy she didn't want to admit, so she could feel like a good colleague while the envy stayed hidden.

qa.q: What turning point made Jyoti's kindness genuine?
qa.a: Admitting on the bus that she was both jealous and glad for Mallika; after that she could congratulate her once, quietly, and really listen.

qa.q: How might Mallika have experienced the biscuits and the repeated congratulations?
qa.a: She may have felt slightly puzzled by so much attention, and more at ease during the hour-long talk that finally felt real.

grounding: An adult notices she has been overly nice to a colleague who won the grant she wanted, admits she is both jealous and glad, and her kindness becomes real.

passage: Dolma, can I tell you something embarrassing? You know Irshad's bakery got written up in the city paper? I've been, like, aggressively supportive. I shared the article nine times. I went on his opening day and told every customer the cinnamon rolls were life-changing. Every time, my jaw ached from smiling. Last night I was about to order twenty rolls for the office, just to prove how happy I was, and I thought: Sahil, who exactly are you proving this to? So I sat on the steps outside my building and made myself say it out loud. "I'm jealous. He did the thing I only talk about." Me, the guy who's been planning a café since college. And then: "And I'm proud of him." Both at once. Weirdly, my shoulders came down. Today I just messaged him, "Proud of you. Honestly a bit jealous too." He sent back, "Ha. Come bake with me on Sunday." I might actually go.

qa.q: How many times did Sahil share the article?
qa.a: Nine times.

qa.q: Why did Sahil's jaw ache from smiling, and what was he feeling underneath?
qa.a: He was forcing extra cheer to cover jealousy, because Irshad had done the thing Sahil only talks about.

qa.q: What choice turned Sahil's support from a performance into something real?
qa.a: Saying out loud that he was both jealous and proud, then sending Irshad one honest message instead of ordering twenty rolls to prove a point.

qa.q: How might Irshad have felt reading 'Honestly a bit jealous too'?
qa.a: Probably touched and closer to Sahil, since the honest line invited a real friendship; the quick invitation to bake suggests he took it warmly. 🙂

grounding: A young man realises his loud support for a friend's bakery is covering envy, admits aloud that he is both jealous and proud, and sends a genuine message.

passage:
I'm Nandini, and I've sat in the same row of cubicles as Sunaina for two years, so I saw the whole thing. When Poornima was made head of the design team, a post Sunaina had wanted, Sunaina started bringing her filter coffee every morning. She praised Poornima's slides in every meeting, sometimes before they had even been shown. It was a lot.
Then on Thursday, in the lift, Sunaina said to me out of nowhere, "I think I'm overdoing it. I'm jealous of her. I'm also really happy for her. Both." She laughed a little.
After that, something changed. The daily coffee stopped. But on Monday, when Poornima's presentation went well, Sunaina said, "That was good," just once, and it sounded like she meant it. Poornima smiled back, a real smile this time.

qa.q: What did Sunaina bring Poornima every morning?
qa.a: Filter coffee.

qa.q: What does Sunaina's comment in the lift suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She was holding two feelings at once, jealousy over the post and real happiness for Poornima, and had noticed her niceness was covering the first.

qa.q: Which choice made Sunaina's praise sound genuine by Monday?
qa.a: Admitting the mixed feeling out loud and dropping the daily coffee, so one simple 'That was good' could carry real meaning.

qa.q: How might Poornima have noticed the change?
qa.a: She probably found the earlier praise a bit much, and could relax into a real smile once Sunaina's words felt honest.

grounding: A colleague watches a woman who was over-sweet to the person promoted above her admit she is both jealous and happy, after which her praise becomes sincere.

passage:
Friday. When Madhuri got the year-long illustration residency in Kyoto, the one Vandana had also applied for, Vandana threw her a surprise party. She hung paper lanterns, made a speech, and bought a set of brushes she couldn't really afford. "You deserve it more than anyone alive!" she said, three times.
Sunday. Cleaning up the lanterns alone, Vandana stopped. She had been nicer to Madhuri this week than in five years of friendship, and none of it had felt warm. It felt like pressing a lid down. She opened her sketchbook and wrote: I'm jealous. I'm also proud of her. Both.
Wednesday. At the chai stall, Vandana said it out loud. "I'm really happy for you. And a bit jealous. Honestly."
Madhuri laughed with relief. "Thank god. You've been so strange." Then, "Sit with me when the next call opens? I'll read your portfolio."

qa.a: I'm jealous. I'm also proud of her. Both.

passage:
"Sahil, you've taken Arjun a gift three weekends in a row since he got that job. Sit. Let your Mehreen phuppo tell you something.
When I was twenty-five, teaching at a girls' school in Hyderabad, my colleague Asma was given the senior post I had wanted badly. From the next week I baked for her every Friday. I praised her lessons in the staff room. I told the principal she was a gift to the school.
One day old Mrs Rao, who taught Urdu, said quietly, 'You praise her like you're paying off a debt.' I was furious. At home I sat on the step and finally said it to myself: I'm jealous, and I'm glad for her. Both are true.
The next Monday I told Asma, 'I wanted that post too. And I'm glad it's you.' She held my hand. Later she asked me to run the debate club with her, and I stopped baking for her. We've been friends for forty years."

qa.q: What did Mrs Rao say about young Mehreen's praise of Asma?
qa.a: "You praise her like you're paying off a debt."

qa.q: Why was young Mehreen baking for Asma every Friday?
qa.a: The extra sweetness covered envy about the senior post that Mehreen didn't want to feel, so being very nice made the resentment seem to vanish.

qa.q: What turning point let Mehreen's kindness become real?
qa.a: Admitting on the step at home that she was both jealous and glad, then telling Asma, "I wanted that post too. And I'm glad it's you."

qa.q: What might Asma have felt on hearing Mehreen's honest words?
qa.a: Asma probably felt trusted and relieved, since an honest mix was easier to believe than weekly baking, and it opened the way to working together.

grounding: Illustrates, through an aunt's memory, an adult who drops her exaggerated niceness toward a resented colleague by admitting envy and gladness together, and becomes a true friend.

passage: Twenty minutes before Hemant's farewell party, Damini was still in the office washroom, rewriting her speech on her phone. Hemant had won the fellowship to Germany, the one she'd also applied for. Her draft said he was "the most brilliant mind I've ever met," "a legend," "a genius who deserves everything." She read it back and winced. It was too much. She'd been extra sweet to him for a week, bringing him chai, laughing at every joke. She leaned against the sink and let herself say it, silently: I'm jealous. And I'm also glad for him. Both. The tight feeling in her chest eased. She deleted the draft and typed something shorter: that he'd helped her debug at midnight twice, that she'd miss arguing with him, and that she hoped to follow him one day. Then she went out, and when she said it, her voice was steady and she meant every word.

qa.q: Where had Hemant won the fellowship to?
qa.a: To Germany.

qa.q: Why did the tight feeling in Damini's chest ease?
qa.a: Once she admitted she was both jealous and glad, she no longer had to hide the envy behind extra sweetness, and she felt calmer and more honest.

qa.q: What makes the second speech better than the first?
qa.a: It is shorter, specific and true, so her kindness is genuine rather than covering resentment.

qa.q: How might Hemant hear Damini's honest speech?
qa.a: Hemant would likely feel touched and respected, hearing real memories rather than empty praise.

grounding: Shows an adult catching herself being extra nice to someone she envies and admitting both envy and happiness, so her kindness becomes genuine.

passage: In her Delhi flat, Ganga was on her third attempt at an elaborate three-layer cake for Pema, whose first novel had just been accepted by a publisher. Ganga had also been writing a novel. For four years. She'd already sent Pema eleven messages that day, all exclamation marks, and planned a surprise party with forty guests. Halfway through piping roses, she stopped. Her hand was shaking. Why was she working this hard? She sat on the kitchen floor and let the truth in: she was envious, sharply, and also proud of Pema, truly. Both at once. She laughed a little, wiped her eyes, and decided the cake could be one layer. Then she wrote a card: "I'm so happy for you. And honestly, a bit jealous. Let's celebrate, and then you can help me finish mine." Pema called her that evening, crying with laughter.

qa.q: How long had Ganga been writing her own novel?
qa.a: For four years.

qa.q: Why did Ganga's hand shake while piping roses?
qa.a: The over-the-top effort was covering envy, and when she noticed, she felt the strain of trying so hard to hide it.

qa.q: Why did Ganga's honest card work?
qa.a: Naming both happiness and envy made her warmth real, and it invited Pema into a closer friendship rather than a performance.

qa.q: How might Pema feel reading the card?
qa.a: Pema likely feels touched and amused, trusting Ganga's happiness more because Ganga admitted the envy.

grounding: Shows an adult noticing her excessive niceness toward a friend's success and admitting she is both envious and happy, which makes her kindness genuine.

passage:
"Akash, want me to iron your shirts for the new hostel? Book the train? Carry your bags?"
"Bhaiya, that's the fifth thing you've offered today. What's going on?"
Saurabh laughed. "Nothing! I'm just happy for you. Top business school, first try."
"You tried twice."
"Yes, well." Saurabh picked up a shirt and put it down. "I'm happy."
"You've been weird all week."
Saurabh sat on the bed. He was quiet for a while. "Okay. The truth? I'm really proud of you. And I'm also jealous. It stings that you got in and I didn't. Both are true."
Akash stared at him. "Oh."
"I'm sorry. I think I was being extra nice to cover it."
Akash grinned slowly. "Thanks for telling me. I'd rather have weird honest bhaiya than fake shirt-ironing bhaiya."
Saurabh laughed, properly this time. "I'll still iron one."

qa.q: How many times did Saurabh try for the business school?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: Why was Saurabh offering to do so many things for Akash?
qa.a: He felt jealous that Akash got in first try, and being extra helpful covered that sting while he tried to show only happiness.

qa.q: What changed when Saurabh named both feelings?
qa.a: The tension eased; his kindness could become genuine, and Akash could trust it.

qa.q: How does Akash feel about his brother's honesty?
qa.a: Akash seems relieved and grateful, preferring an honest brother to a falsely cheerful one.

grounding: Shows an adult catching himself being overly nice to a brother he envies, admitting both pride and envy so his kindness becomes genuine.

passage:
I'm Bhupen, and for a week after Gautam got into the Edinburgh master's programme, I was the nicest friend alive. I organised the farewell dinner. I made a slideshow. I told everyone, "I'm SO happy for him," maybe twenty times. And every night I went home with a tight chest, scrolling his acceptance post.

On Thursday, halfway through ironing a shirt for the dinner, I stopped and said it out loud in my empty room: "I'm jealous. I applied last year and didn't get in. And I'm also glad for him." Both. Same time.

Strangely, the tightness loosened. At the dinner I didn't make a speech. I just hugged Gautam and said, "I'm a bit envious, honestly. And really proud of you." He laughed and said, "I'd be envious too." It was the most real thing I'd said all week.

qa.q: Which programme did Gautam get into?
qa.a: Gautam got into the Edinburgh master's programme.

qa.q: Why did Bhupen go home each night with a tight chest?
qa.a: Bhupen was envious, having been turned down the year before, and the extra-sweet gestures were covering that feeling rather than easing it.

qa.q: What changed things for Bhupen, and why?
qa.a: Saying out loud that the jealousy and the gladness were both true loosened the tightness, so the words at dinner became honest and warm.

qa.q: How might Gautam have felt hearing Bhupen's honest words?
qa.a: Gautam seemed touched and at ease, laughing and admitting he'd feel the same, which made the friendship feel closer.

grounding: An adult looks back on being extra nice to a friend while envious, then admitting both envy and joy so the kindness becomes real.

passage:
Supervisor's note, design team, 12 October.

Since Pallavi's portfolio was picked for the national showcase, Tejas has been unusually sweet to her. He fetched her coffee three days running, praised her in every stand-up, and offered to format her slides at eleven at night. The praise sounded bright but a little brittle. Tejas had submitted to the same showcase.

Today in our one-to-one, before I said anything, he said, "I've been overdoing it with Pallavi. The truth is I'm envious. And I'm also genuinely happy for her. Both." He looked relieved to have said it.

This afternoon I saw him give her feedback on her talk: two real suggestions, one honest compliment, no coffee. She took notes. I'd call it the most useful help he has given her all week.

R. Menon

qa.q: How many days running did Tejas fetch Pallavi's coffee?
qa.a: Tejas fetched her coffee three days running.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling underneath the bright praise?
qa.a: Tejas felt envious, having submitted to the same showcase, and also genuinely happy for Pallavi; the extra sweetness covered the envy.

qa.q: Why was the afternoon feedback better help than the coffee?
qa.a: Once Tejas admitted both feelings, the kindness could be honest: real suggestions and a true compliment actually helped Pallavi's talk.

qa.q: How might Pallavi experience the change in Tejas?
qa.a: Pallavi probably finds the honest feedback more useful and easier to trust than the brittle praise, which is why she took notes.

grounding: A supervisor's note shows a young man who admits envy alongside real happiness for a colleague, after which his help becomes genuine.

passage:
Sunday night

Lalit's housewarming today. I brought the biggest sweets box in the shop, helped carry chairs for two hours, and told his parents three times what a smart choice the flat was. Very generous of me. Also very fake.

Because on the way home in the auto I finally admitted it: I'm envious. Lalit and I started work the same year. He has a flat with a balcony. I have a rented room with a leaking tap. That stings.

And I'm happy for him. Really. He worked for years for this. His mother cried when she lit the lamp.

Both are true. Writing it here makes the jealousy smaller, not bigger. Next weekend I'll help him put up his shelves, and this time it won't be a show.

Yusuf

qa.q: How long did Yusuf help carry chairs?
qa.a: Yusuf helped carry chairs for two hours.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling on the way home in the auto?
qa.a: Yusuf felt envious and stung, comparing the balcony flat with a rented room, while also being truly happy for Lalit.

qa.q: What did writing the diary do for Yusuf?
qa.a: Naming both feelings made the jealousy smaller, so the next help, putting up shelves, can be genuine rather than a show.

qa.q: How might Lalit's mother have felt at the housewarming?
qa.a: Lalit's mother seemed deeply moved and proud, crying as she lit the lamp in the new flat.

grounding: A diary shows an adult noticing fake generosity at a friend's housewarming and admitting both envy and gladness.

passage: In the small town of Bagalkot, Urmila's new tailoring shop had opened opposite Jahnavi's, and within a month half of Jahnavi's customers had crossed the road. Jahnavi found herself taking Urmila sweets every other day, praising her stitching to everyone, laughing a little too loudly at her jokes. One evening, walking home past the temple, she caught herself rehearsing yet another compliment, and stopped. "I'm jealous," she said quietly to the dark road. "And I actually like her." Saying both made her chest loosen. The next morning she didn't take sweets. She went across and said, "Your blouse designs are better than mine. Teach me that neckline? I'll teach you my hemming." Urmila grinned and pulled up a stool.

qa.q: How quickly did half of Jahnavi's customers cross the road?
qa.a: Within a month.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi feel when she stopped on the road?
qa.a: She admitted she felt jealous of Urmila and also that she liked her; saying both made her chest loosen with relief.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi do differently the next morning?
qa.a: Instead of sweets and overdone praise, she honestly admired Urmila's designs and offered to swap skills.

qa.a: Pleased and welcomed, grinning and pulling up a stool, glad of a real friend across the road.

passage:
At the clinic where they both worked as physiotherapists, Swati's engagement photos went round the staff room on Monday. Nazia was the loudest. "Gorgeous! You two are perfect!" She offered to cover Swati's Thursday shift, bought her a coffee and praised the ring three times before noon. By lunch her cheeks ached from smiling.
Rolling up a resistance band in the empty gym, she finally let herself think it: I'm jealous. Swati found someone, and I'm still being asked at every family dinner when I'll settle down. And I'm glad for her too. Both.
The breath she let out felt like her first real one all day. That afternoon, when Swati thanked her again, Nazia said simply, "I'm really happy for you. And a little envious, honestly."
Swati laughed and hugged her. "Envious is allowed."

qa.q: Which shift did Nazia offer to cover?
qa.a: Swati's Thursday shift.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling beneath the loud compliments?
qa.a: She was both envious and genuinely glad for Swati 😊; admitting the jealousy brought relief, like her first real breath all day.

qa.q: Why did admitting the mixed feeling help?
